messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Special Education Teacher
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Authority Presence: Police
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was thirty-two when he was attacked outside the grocery store three blocks from his apartment in Portland. It was a Tuesday evening in November, the kind of ordinary moment that would later feel impossible to reconcile with what followed. He had been walking home from work, still in the khakis and polo shirt he wore to the special education classroom where he taught eight- and nine-year-olds with learning disabilities. Two men emerged from between the parked cars. One of them shouted at him—a sharp, aggressive command to give them his wallet. Marcus remembered the exact timbre of that voice, the way it had seemed to come from everywhere at once, bouncing off the storefronts and the pavement. He had frozen. One of the men grabbed him from behind, his forearm pressing hard against Marcus's neck, cutting off air. Marcus had struggled, had tried to turn, and the man had wrenched his arm higher, the pressure building in his throat, in his head. He had given them what they wanted. They ran. He stood there alone on the sidewalk, gasping, his neck screaming with pain.

Three years had passed since that evening, and Marcus had not recovered. The attack had left him with a chronic ache in his neck—a dull, persistent reminder that lived in the back of his skull and the upper trapezius. Some days it was barely noticeable; other days it felt like a hand was still there, still pressing. When someone raised their voice—a student in class, a colleague in the hallway, a stranger on the street—Marcus's body would flood with the certainty that violence was imminent. His nervous system did not distinguish between a frustrated parent on the phone and the man who had shouted at him that night. Shouting meant danger. Shouting meant he was about to lose control of his own body.

The presence of police officers triggered something different but equally destabilizing. When a police car pulled up near his apartment complex, or when an officer appeared in the hallway at school for a safety assembly, Marcus felt his chest tighten. He had come to believe that authority figures—people with power, people with the capacity to restrain him—were fundamentally unsafe. He could not articulate why, exactly, but the association had calcified over the three years into something that felt like absolute truth.

What frightened Marcus most was that he could not relax. Even in his own apartment, with the door locked and the lights on, he remained vigilant. He scanned the windows, checked the locks repeatedly, and when he entered any space—the grocery store, the school building, a restaurant—he immediately identified the exits. This had become automatic, so ingrained that he was often not consciously aware he was doing it until he noticed his eyes moving, his body angling toward the nearest door. At school, his hypervigilance had begun to affect his teaching. He found it harder to focus on the lesson plans, harder to give his students the patient attention they needed, because part of his mind was always monitoring the room, watching for threats that his rational mind knew were not coming.

When Marcus allowed himself to remember what had happened, the memory came with crystalline, unbearable clarity. He could see the exact angle of the man's face as he shouted, could feel the texture of the pavement beneath his feet, could hear the distant sound of a car horn blocks away. The vividness of it was both a curse and a strange kind of torture—it made the event feel present, happening now, not three years in the past. And with the memory came rage so intense it frightened him. He would clench his fists, his jaw, his entire body would tense with a fury that had nowhere to go. Sometimes he would punch his pillow. Sometimes he would sit in his car in the school parking lot after work and just shake with anger at himself—at the man he had been that evening, the man who had been careless enough to be on that street at that time, the man who had not fought back hard enough, the man who had simply handed over his wallet like a coward. Somebody else would have done something different. Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation in the first place.

Marcus had taken a leave from teaching two months ago. The constant monitoring, the inability to relax even in the presence of children who depended on him, the intrusive memories that would arrive without warning—it had become unsustainable. He had started having panic attacks. The guilt that accompanied his memories had begun to feel unbearable, a weight that pressed down on him daily. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally inadequate, that he lacked whatever it took to move through the world safely. When his sister finally insisted he see someone, he had agreed, not with hope, but with the desperate understanding that he could not continue as he was.
